title: The Faintest Line
subtitle: A shift on the dye district railway
story:
This city's dye district made colours for two hundred years. When the trade died, the railway beneath the district went dark, but the lichen emerged: orange and grey-green, creeping across the old tile.

Your biotechnology company scrapes the lichen off the tunnel walls and sells it on today's boutique pigment market. You have two jobs today. First, work out which gene in the lichen's genome controls pigment abundance. Then find somewhere new to grow the lichen: places on the network that no train has stopped at in decades.

Ride the lines. Keep your eyes open.

done.title: The assay is filed
done.body: The regulator is named, and it is the quietest gene on the wall — nine seasons of re-seeding from the heaviest growth were nine seasons of re-seeding from a bystander. The works can breed for colour again, from a strand nobody would have picked up.

escapeDone.title: There is a great deal of wall down there
escapeDone.body: Two platforms that were on no map are on the record, fixed off nothing but the hops you rode and what you saw go past. The standing order was bigger than the growing face; it is bigger again now. The river has the low tunnels — but the survey holds, and the ebb was enough.

puzzleQueue.label: The driving desk — the reference pair
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 1 · pairwise correlation. ANSWER XAN_4574 (|r| 0.832 vs 0.079 for the runner-up, 10.5x). The probe is deliberately a SATELLITE pair — probing inside the pigment module would return XAN_1192 and spoil the boss. Correct index 2.

question.prompt:
The works keeps one strand as its reference: XAN_4418. Its behaviour is trusted, and the standing note in every cab says it never moves alone — something on the crop always moves with it, and no one has written down what.

The assay sheets under the clip on this desk are the whole crop record: two hundred samples, twenty-four genes, one expression reading each.

Which gene tracks XAN_4418 most closely across the samples?

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: XAN_4574 tracks the reference strand XAN_4418, |r| 0.83.
wrong: Correlate every other gene's expression against XAN_4418's across all two hundred samples, then rank by the size of the correlation — its sign does not matter here, only its magnitude.

One pair stands well clear of the rest: the winner is above 0.8 while every other gene falls below 0.1. If your answer sits somewhere in that crowd below 0.1, you have picked something out of the noise.
Check you correlated against XAN_4418 itself. The strongest pair anywhere in this dataset does not involve XAN_4418 at all, and two of the options belong to it.

puzzleQueue.label: The driving desk — the control strand
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 2 · threshold + one-vs-all. ANSWER XAN_6246, the sole isolate at |r|>0.75 (its strongest tie to anything is 0.103). THE THRESHOLD IS STATED IN THE PROMPT ON PURPOSE — the answer is stable only over |r| 0.15-0.7569; at 0.76 XAN_1815 and XAN_2781 also become isolates and the rung has three answers. NO HINT MAY SUGGEST A CUTOFF ABOVE 0.75. Correct index 0.

question.prompt:
Before the works will trust an assay it wants a control: a strand that answers to nothing else on the crop, so a reading off it means the instrument and not the culture.

Two genes count as co-expressed here when the magnitude of their correlation exceeds 0.75.

Which gene has no co-expression partners at all?

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: XAN_6246 is the control strand, with no partners at |r| > 0.75.
wrong: For each gene, count how many of the other twenty-three it is co-expressed with at a magnitude above 0.75. The control is the one whose count comes out at zero.
Several genes have exactly one partner, and one partner is not the same as none — if your answer has a single strong tie, it is a near miss rather than the control.

Hold the threshold at 0.75 as given. The control is isolated by a wide margin — its strongest tie to anything is barely above 0.1 — while several other genes sit just the other side of the line and would drift in and out if you moved it.

puzzleQueue.label: The driving desk — the works' standing practice
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 3 · module + abundance. THE TAUGHT TRAP. ANSWER XAN_1815 (1434 units vs 245 for the next in module, 5.9x) — which has DEGREE 1. This is the method the works has re-seeded by for nine seasons while the colour thinned, and rung 4 is its correction. Correct index 5.

question.prompt:
The works has re-seeded from the same strand for nine seasons and the colour has thinned every one of them. The practice is written into the standing orders, and it has never been questioned: take the pigment module — the block of genes that rise and fall together with pigment production — and re-seed from whichever of them runs most abundant.

Which gene does that practice pick?

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: the standing practice picks XAN_1815, the most abundant gene in the pigment module at ~1434 units.
wrong: Recover the module first — the block of genes co-expressed with one another above 0.75 that pigment production sits inside — and only then compare average expression, within that block alone.

Stay inside the module. The loudest genes in the whole crop record run above 5000 units and are not members of it; if your answer is one of those, you ranked across everything instead of within the block.
Inside the module it is not close: the winner averages around 1400 units where the next one down is under 250.

puzzleQueue.label: The driving desk — the regulator
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 4 · BOSS. module + network position. ANSWER XAN_1192 — the LOWEST-expressed gene in the dataset (71.5 units, rank 24 of 24), co-expressed with EVERY other member of its module (degree 7 vs 4 for the next). Decoy XAN_3514: loudest in the transcriptome at 5644 units, degree 3, and not even in the module. Correct index 3.

question.prompt:
Nine seasons of re-seeding by abundance have thinned the colour, so abundance is plainly not what governs it. Something in that module is setting the level for the rest, and it is the strand the others answer to rather than the strand that shouts loudest.

Which gene regulates pigment production?

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: XAN_1192 regulates pigment production — the quietest gene in the whole record at ~72 units, yet tied to every other gene in its module.
wrong: Work inside the pigment module again, but rank its members by position rather than by size: for each one, count how many other members it is co-expressed with above 0.75.
The regulator is tied to every other member of its module and nothing else in the block comes close. Abundance will never find it — it is the quietest gene in the entire record.

If your answer is the loudest gene in the crop record, that is the bystander this whole assay exists to rule out: it runs at more than seventy times the regulator and is not even a member of the module.

debrief.title: How this railway worked
debrief.intro: Two networks, and they had nothing to do with each other. The genes' network you built yourself — correlate, threshold, read. The rails' network was handed to you as observed fact, one ride at a time, and you could only ever know the parts of it you had been down. Both times the loudest thing was not the most connected thing.

worldPlatePrompt: A wide establishing view inside a Victorian underground railway that stood derelict for a century and is now being worked again as a lichen farm. TIME-NEUTRAL soft even underground light, neither dawn nor dusk, no daylight in this frame. THE CROP IS THE ARCHITECTURE, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING IN THE FRAME: the lichen grows ON THE FABRIC OF THE TUNNEL ITSELF, not in containers — thick living sheets of flat orange rosettes and swollen grey-green crusts spreading across the glazed wall tile, climbing the pilasters and furring the brick soffits of the arches overhead, so the walls themselves are visibly alive and shaggy with it. It is a crop growing on a building. Galvanised racking and plastic trays of cut crust stand about as the HARVEST TAKEN OFF THOSE WALLS — the product, never the source. Nothing is cultivated in a tray. THE FABRIC UNDER IT IS OLD AND DAMAGED: glazed brick and tile in ochre, saffron and dirty cream, much of it crazed, chipped or missing with the bedding mortar showing through; paint peeling in sheets off cast-iron columns; rust and water stains bleeding down; perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators; sooted segmental brick arches; granite platform edges worn hollow. A CREW WORKS HERE NOW, VISIBLY AND WELL: cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex strung along the arches, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, a kettle and enamel mugs on a plank shelf, a coat on a hook, and notices, work rotas, tally sheets and curling postcards tacked and taped to the tile with chalked marks and scratched tallies beside them. Repairs done with ingenuity — a propped timber, a patched panel, a hose run into a channel. TWO COLOUR TEMPERATURES, AND BOTH MUST BE STRONGLY PRESENT — this must NOT be a monochrome amber or sepia picture. WARM: pools of amber lamplight around the work-lamps and the crew's corner. COLD: everywhere the lamps do not reach, a distinct COLD BLUE-GREEN DAMP — wet black tile going blue in the shadow, green-black standing water, cold blue-green light down the tunnel mouths and in the depths of the arches, the chill of a place with a river behind the wall. The cold blue-green should occupy at least as much of the frame as the warm amber, and the two should meet in clear contrast rather than blending into brown. Damp air, faint haze, film grain. Photographic and beautiful. THE MOOD IS WARM, PURPOSEFUL AND CHARACTERFUL — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. It is emphatically NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin. Dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom for its own sake, no horror atmosphere of any kind. No large blank empty wall areas — every surface carries the marks and clutter of a working place. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text, no signage or readable writing of any kind anywhere. No sepia monochrome, no uniform brown or orange cast over the whole image.
coverPrompt: A bold, graphic, MID-TO-HIGH-KEY square poster in flat vector-poster shapes. A single Victorian underground railway arch seen head-on and filling most of the frame, its opening a LARGE GLOWING field of warm amber lamplight — the brightest thing in the picture and the first thing the eye finds. Growing across that glowing arch, in strong flat silhouette, a bold band of LICHEN: fat round orange rosettes and a ragged grey-green crust spreading in from the arch's rim and over the tilework, deliberately oversized and simplified so it still reads at the size of a postage stamp. Two rails run out of the arch toward the viewer as two clean converging lines. The surround is a cool blue-green tile field, MID-TONE — clearly darker than the arch but never black. Three values only: bright amber, mid blue-green, and the orange crop. Big simple shapes, few of them, strong edges. NOT a dark or murky picture: no near-black fields, no deep shadow, no gloom, nothing dim, and no photographic haze — this is a printed poster, not a photograph of a tunnel. Square. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text, no logos.

sceneSpec.atmosphere: wet, green and echoing, patinated copper under a cold cab lamp, everything running, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake

authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from the DRIVER'S CABIN at the head of the works' heavy black iron unit, the only one never taken out of service on an underground works railway — the viewer is standing IN the cab itself at the controls, its walls wrapping right around them, the gangway door to the car behind at one end and the forward window over the driving desk at the other. This is an EQUIRECTANGULAR 360 panorama, not a flat photograph: the walls wrap continuously right around the viewer with strong barrel curvature, the ceiling and floor bow across the frame, and any surface toward the left or right of the frame is at the viewer's SIDE, seen at a glancing angle rather than face-on. It is NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, there is no single-vanishing-point composition, and it is never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. On the far left, the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, the left half of that one quiet stretch; to the left, the rear end of the cab: an offset gangway door in the rear bulkhead, glazed in its upper half, showing the cage-wagon behind, seen through the glass — no seats, heavy barred sides, a bare planked floor worn to a shine and the tunnel dark showing between the bars — a view through only; it is shut; just left of centre, a scuffed grey speaker jammed into a bulkhead bracket and held with cable ties, its grille clearly visible and a charging lead trailing — plainly the driver's own, and newer than everything around it; dead ahead in the centre, the cab's side door out to the platform, directly ahead of the viewer, its upper half a large panel of FROSTED ribbed glass — translucent and completely opaque to detail, so nothing whatever of what lies beyond it can be made out, only a soft even glow coming through; just right of centre, a soot-blackened iron driving desk with a massive master controller, a worn brake handle, two round gauges with plain unmarked dials, and a hinged writing-flap folded down at its left end carrying the works' assay sheets under a bulldog clip; just right of centre, a cast-iron destination selector on a short pedestal at the outboard end of the driving desk, a heavy brass pointer standing over a ring of blank enamel plates, none of them marked; to the right, the front end of the cab: its single large forward window above the desk, looking straight along the running rails — the twin rails converging away into the black of the tunnel, the brick tunnel ring lit by the unit's own headlamp and a receding string of small lamps dwindling to a point; on the far right, the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, the right half of that one quiet stretch, joining its other half. heavy, dark and grinding, soot-black iron under one caged bulb, deep shadow, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake. This is an EQUIRECTANGULAR 360 panorama, not a flat photograph: the walls wrap continuously right around the viewer with strong barrel curvature, the ceiling and floor bow across the frame, and any surface toward the left or right of the frame is at the viewer's SIDE, seen at a glancing angle rather than face-on. NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, no single-vanishing-point composition, and never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text, no signage, no readable writing of any kind, no destination names, no daylight. EXACTLY ONE opening in the cab shows anything beyond it moving — the forward window at the RIGHT. The side door dead ahead is FROSTED and no platform, station, tile, lamp or figure is visible through it. Behind the viewer is a SOLID BLIND WALL with no window, porthole or opening of any kind. There is NO door at the front of the cab — the front is a window only. The image is SHARP: no motion blur, no streaking, no smeared or doubled detail anywhere — everything in this picture is standing still, and any movement described is what the cinemagraph will add later, never something painted into the still. THE TRACKWAY IS NEVER FLOODED: wherever running rails appear they and their track bed are clear and usable, with no water standing over them, and there is no canal, waterway or navigable channel anywhere in the station — any water lies as shallow sheets or in a shallow drainage channel at the platform foot, never on the rails. The cab fittings are rigid: nothing slides, tips, rolls or drifts. No large blank empty wall areas anywhere — every surface carries the marks and clutter of a working place. Nothing eerie, spooky, creepy, haunted or menacing; no cobwebs, no horror atmosphere. Again: the extreme left and right edges must align perfectly into the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, with no visible seam, join, or repetition.
